concept_options.title: The Sky Should Be Violet
concept_options.hook: Violet light scatters MORE than blue. So why isn't the sky violet? Check your own eyes.
concept_options.visual_approach: Flat motion graphics on a deep-slate background that gradually shifts from violet to sky blue as the explanation lands. Animated text cards for the paradox, a wavelength bar chart for the scattering ratios, and a cone-sensitivity beat rendered as a stat/comparison card. Sunset gradient finale.
concept_options.target_audience: Curious general audience who already 'know' the Rayleigh answer
key_points: Rayleigh scattering scales with 1/wavelength^4 — blue scatters ~6-10x more than red
Violet scatters even more than blue, yet the sky is not violet
Three reasons: the sun emits less violet, the upper atmosphere absorbs some, and human blue cones dominate perception
Sunsets are the same physics with a longer light path
concept_options.core_message: The sky's color is decided partly in the atmosphere and partly inside your own eyes.
concept_options.cta: Next time you watch a sunset, remember: same physics, longer path.
concept_options.why_this_works: The violet paradox is the top unanswered audience question in this topic's short-form landscape; no surveyed video animates the three-part answer, and 'the answer is in your eyes' is a genuine information gap.

concept_options.title: The Fourth-Power Law That Paints the Sky
concept_options.hook: One tiny equation explains blue skies, red sunsets, and pale horizons all at once.
concept_options.visual_approach: Data-led motion graphics: animated 1/lambda^4 formula card, count-up stat cards (5.9x blue vs red), and a bar chart of scattering intensity by color. Ends with three-way payoff cards: sky, sunset, horizon.
concept_options.target_audience: STEM-curious viewers who want the quantitative why
key_points: Blue (~450nm) scatters roughly 6-10x more than red (~700nm)
The same law explains sunsets (longer path) and pale horizons (multiple scattering)
concept_options.core_message: A single power law paints every color you see in the sky.
concept_options.cta: One equation, three sky phenomena — physics is efficient.
concept_options.why_this_works: The quantitative angle is underused: existing content says 'blue scatters more' without ever showing how much. Count-up stat cards make the ~6x blue-vs-red figure viscerally satisfying.

concept_options.title: It Took 52 Years to Answer a Child's Question
concept_options.hook: Every 4-year-old asks why the sky is blue. It took Tyndall, Rayleigh, AND Einstein to answer.
concept_options.visual_approach: Timeline-driven motion graphics: 1859 -> 1871 -> 1911 date cards with each scientist's contribution as an animated callout; closes on the modern one-line answer.
key_points: Tyndall discovered blue-preferential scattering experimentally in 1859
Rayleigh derived the fourth-power law in 1871
Einstein's 1911 calculation settled that air molecules themselves do the scattering
concept_options.core_message: Simple questions can take generations of genius to answer properly.
concept_options.cta: What other 'simple' questions are secretly deep?
concept_options.why_this_works: The 52-year discovery arc ending with Einstein is absent from every popular explainer surveyed — a genuine surprise for viewers who think this is settled kid-science.

selected_concept.rationale: Autonomous cloud run (user request was open-ended: 'make a video'). c1 selected because it has the strongest hook grounded in the #1 underserved gap, its myth-busting structure differentiates from the saturated one-liner landscape, and its visual beats (paradox card, scattering bar chart, cone-sensitivity comparison, sunset finale) map perfectly onto the free Remotion component stack — maximum quality at $0.00.
modifications: Absorb c2's quantitative beat: include the 1/lambda^4 bar chart and the ~5.9x stat card (blue vs red) as the setup before the violet paradox
Close with c2's sunset payoff as the CTA beat

Both runtimes were presented in the user-facing summary per the HARD RULE; selection made autonomously because this is a cloud run with no interactive approval channel.
